title: What if the ocean hit 122°F? 🌀
subject: hurricane
description:
How far inland would you need to run? 👇

What is a hypercane? In 1995, MIT's Kerry Emanuel and NCAR's Richard Rotunno simulated hurricanes over ocean water heated to about 122°F by an asteroid impact or undersea eruption. The winds topped 500 mph. The hottest seawater ever measured, 101.1°F off Florida in 2023, is still about 21 degrees short.

Sources: Emanuel, Speer, Rotunno, Srivastava & Molina 1995, "Hypercanes: A possible link in global extinction scenarios", Journal of Geophysical Research 100(D7):13755-13765; Christian Science Monitor (10 Oct 1995, "Could 'Superhurricanes' Have Done In Dinosaurs?"); NOAA / AP via PBS NewsHour (Manatee Bay buoy, 24 July 2023); NOAA National Hurricane Center, Hurricane Patricia report

scenes.text: 500 mph winds would need a 122°F ocean.
MIT's Kerry Emanuel modeled that storm in 1995 and called it a hypercane. An asteroid or undersea eruption would have to heat the sea.
The hottest sea water ever measured was 101.1°F, off Florida's Manatee Bay in July 2023.
Hurricane Patricia, the strongest on record, peaked at 215 mph.
A hypercane's clouds would climb 20 miles, and scientists think its water could thin the ozone layer.
Today's oceans are still 21°F too cool.
